routes.description: Analytic idealism reduces reality to consciousness, the sole pre-theoretical given, while treating physicality as a perceptual representation of external mental states.
routes.successCriteria: Show that this ontology explains conscious experience, an objective structured world, and causal regularity more parsimoniously than an ontology containing nonmental matter.

motionBridge.description: Consciousness is the ontological foundation rather than an emergent product of matter.

centralBridges.description: Consciousness is the sole directly given category and additional nonmental categories require justification.
Physical properties are representations of mind-independent external mental states.
Intrinsic dispositions of external mental states can ground causal and physical regularity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Strong emergence from nonconscious quantities lacks an intelligible explanatory bridge.
Dissociative boundaries distinguish individual minds from the wider field of mentality.

routes.description: Neutral monism avoids substance dualism and the hard problem without identifying the unknown underlying reality specifically as consciousness or mentality.
routes.successCriteria: Show that idealism adds no warranted explanation of objective structure, representation, boundaries, or causation beyond a neutral monist account.

motionBridge.description: Neutral monism is sufficient, so consciousness need not be declared reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: The underlying monistic reality should remain ontologically neutral where its nature is unknown.
An adequate ontology must explain the objective world's stable structure and regularities.
Consciousness talk can be reframed in terms of representations without positing a separate substance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Idealism must explain the boundary between private and external states rather than merely name it.
Idealism must identify the source of causal organization within its proposed mental substrate.

sections.title: Foundational ontology and explanatory burden
sections.rationale: The opening clash establishes both sides' ontological routes and the principal burden concerning emergence, neutrality, and explanatory structure.

sections.title: External reality as representation
sections.rationale: This exchange tests whether idealism preserves a mind-independent world and whether calling its substrate mental explains anything further.

sections.title: Explanatory economy and the hard problem
sections.rationale: The moves compare idealism's removal of nonmental ontology with the objection that this maneuver may relocate rather than resolve explanation.

sections.title: Boundaries, causation, and physical regularity
sections.rationale: This section bears directly on whether dissociation and intrinsic dispositions can account for organisms, causation, and predictable physical structure.

sections.title: Representational models and experience
sections.rationale: The final selected exchange tests the neutral-monist representational proposal and idealism's claim that experienced models still presuppose mentality.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical datum, so reduction should begin from consciousness as a type of existence rather than add an inferred substrate.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly addresses Bernardo immediately before this uninterrupted first-person answer, and the position matches his assigned side.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive statement of the pro route and has no earlier selected argumentative target available in source chronology.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly establishes the adopted starting point and reductionist rationale, though the exclusivity inference remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The datum, reduction, and consciousness-as-type claims are recoverable, with the limits of the methodological preference left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The methodological preference is intelligible, but direct givenness alone does not fully establish ontological priority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reductionist route is stable, but moving from epistemic givenness to ontological priority requires an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Direct acquaintance supplies relevant support, while the claim that it fixes ontology remains principally philosophical assertion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central bridge identifying consciousness as the privileged ontological starting point.

representationalCharity.rationale: No live opposing alternative is represented or attacked within this opening span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span contains the complete reductionist argument from the pre-theoretical datum to consciousness as the proposed basic category.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Strong emergence of qualitative experience from nonconscious physical quantities is explanatorily empty because no deduction connects physical parameters to experiential qualities.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted answer continues under Bernardo's direct response to the moderator and expressly defends the pro position.

response.rationale: No earlier selected con move exists, so this remains constructive despite presenting contrary material against emergent physicalism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It states a clear explanatory objection and identifies the missing qualitative deduction with substantial directness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly limited to strong emergence from a nonconscious substrate and identifies the alleged missing bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explanatory-gap argument is forceful, but declaring emergentism false exceeds what failure of a current deduction alone establishes.

charity.alternative: Strong emergence holds that consciousness arises from a nonconscious physical substrate.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move specifically addresses strong emergence and its demanded bridge from quantities to qualities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent semantic or deductive grounding to explanatory failure is coherent, though not a categorical disproof.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quantities-to-qualities contrast supports the objection, but no developed emergentist account is examined comparatively.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances a necessary subsidiary bridge by attacking the principal emergence alternative to the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The target is fairly limited to strong emergence, although possible non-deductive physicalist warrants are not developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span states the strong-emergence target, explains why merely naming emergence lacks content, and specifies the quantitative-to-qualitative gap.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Neutral monism accepts the hard problem's force and rejects dualism, but the unknown underlying unity need not be identified as mental.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Susan, whose extended first-person statement defines her disagreement and neutral-monist stance.

response.rationale: Although it contrasts with the pro case, the span develops Susan's own neutral-monist route without component-level contact to one selected earlier move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly stakes out the alternative route, but its positive account of the neutral underlying unity remains deliberately underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: Neutral monism is clear as a refusal of dualism, but the nature and explanatory commitments of the neutral substrate remain unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly acknowledges not knowing what the single underlying reality is and advances only a cautious alternative.

charity.alternative: Analytic idealism proposes that everything is mental and uses dissociation to explain apparent plurality.
charity.decisiveQualification: She acknowledges idealism as a serious monist attempt and shares its criticism of matter-to-consciousness emergence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Withholding a mental designation is coherent, but the route supplies only a thin positive explanation of the neutral unity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hard-problem history and neural-correlate discussion are relevant, while the neutral alternative receives little independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the complete con conclusion that monism need not identify consciousness as foundational.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately grants idealism's monist strength and shared objections before locating the disagreement over going fully idealist.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span develops the hard-problem background, grants substantial common ground, and states the refusal to proceed from monism to full idealism.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism's dissociation analogy does not explain why the world divides and behaves with its observed physical structure.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan continues her explicitly invited explanation of why she does not accept Bernardo's idealist conclusion.

components.text: Consciousness is the privileged simple category from which reality should be reduced.
Beginning from the pre-theoretical datum yields a preferable explanatory account of nature.

response.rationale: The reply challenges the claimed explanatory preference by identifying missing accounts of division and structure, then contrasts this with physical structural explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive explanatory-preference inference, though the comparison to material explanations remains broad and tentative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criticism is clearly confined to the dissociation account's explanatory adequacy for division and physical structure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the objection as failure to follow or find answers rather than claiming a categorical refutation.

charity.alternative: Idealism models individual minds as dissociated alters within a universal mentality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy is acknowledged as interesting before its explanatory adequacy is challenged.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand that ontological labeling explain observed differentiation and order directly tests the pro route's comparative claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed physical regularity motivates the objection, but the rival physical explanation is referenced only at a general level.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally advances the con requirement that an ontology explain stable objective structure.

representationalCharity.rationale: It identifies the dissociation proposal accurately and concedes its interest before articulating the missing explanatory work.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span gives the explicit reason for rejecting full idealism: unexplained division and inadequate accounting for the physical world's structure.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism preserves an external, observer-independent world by treating physical perception as representation of external mental states, not as creation by personal minds.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo explicitly resumes after Susan's question and carefully distinguishes his private mental contents from the external world's mental states.

components.text: Idealism must preserve a world whose existence and behavior do not depend on individual wishes.
Idealism must explain how an external structured world differs from private experience.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes private from external mentality and explains physical qualities as perceptual representations of inaccessible external states.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers both indispensable components explicitly, although the mechanism producing detailed structure is not yet fully supplied.

precisionFindings.rationale: Personal mental contents, external mental states, and perceptual representations are repeatedly and consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move primarily explicates what the idealist model entails rather than claiming decisive empirical confirmation.

charity.alternative: The objection assumes idealism may deny or subjectivize the external world.
charity.decisiveQualification: The response preserves the legitimate demand for an external world while denying that externality requires nonmental substance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The private-external distinction and representation relation form a coherent answer with one remaining bridge concerning detailed structure.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analogy with access to another person's thoughts supports conceptual possibility, but does not independently verify universal mentality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially establishes the central pro bridge that physicality can represent mind-independent external mental states.

representationalCharity.rationale: It isolates the strongest external-world concern and answers it without portraying the objection as a denial of representation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contains the full distinction between private and external mental states and the claim that physical qualities are perceptual representations.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible external substrate mental adds no clear explanation of the representations or the machinery that constructs them.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan immediately responds in first person to Bernardo's external-mental-state account and frames a direct explanatory objection.

components.text: External mental states exist independently and are inaccessible except through perceptual representation.
Labeling those represented states mental avoids adding a separate ontological category.
The account must explain the origin and construction of structured representations.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the inaccessibility claim but argues that the mental label neither specifies the substrate nor explains predictive representational machinery.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the core ontology and representation claims and states the decisive consequence that explanatory work remains undone.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criticism consistently concerns explanatory addition, substrate, and representational construction rather than external-world existence itself.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly presents uncertainty about what the mental designation adds instead of asserting its impossibility.

charity.alternative: External physicality is a representation of observer-independent mental states inaccessible in themselves.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply accepts representationalism and targets the further identification of the represented substrate as mental.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between relabeling a substrate and explaining representational construction is clear and directly consequential.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Predictive processing provides a relevant explanatory demand, though the move does not develop a complete neutral-monist mechanism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks a central pro bridge by disputing the explanatory value of external mentality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves Bernardo's external-world and representational commitments while targeting only the added mental ontology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span states the inaccessible-substrate objection and asks what constructs representations and what explanatory gain the mental label supplies.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Idealism gains explanatory economy by removing the unnecessary nonmental category whose alleged production of mentality creates the hard problem.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo answers Susan's immediately preceding challenge and explicitly states what identifying the substrate as mental adds.

components.text: Calling the external substrate mental must add explanatory value rather than merely rename it.
The account must explain how external states affect and generate internal representations.

response.rationale: The reply identifies ontological economy as the added value and sketches direct mental-to-mental causation as the representation mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers both components clearly, though the dissociation premise and evolutionary story remain only briefly warranted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The economy and mental-to-mental causation claims are clear, while the standards for calling the nonmental category unnecessary remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Avoiding one explanatory gap is a real advantage, but the claim that the alternative is impossible is stronger than the supplied argument.

charity.alternative: A neutral or nonmental substrate may underlie representations without being reducible to mentality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply addresses the demand for explanatory gain rather than treating representationalism itself as the disagreement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Removing a category that creates a cross-category gap is coherent, but simplicity does not alone establish the remaining ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Everyday mental-to-mental modulation illustrates coherence, while universal dissociation and external causation remain speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply centrally defends the claimed parsimony of beginning with consciousness rather than a nonmental substrate.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the objection as a demand for explanatory addition, though it characterizes the rival category as unnecessary without full comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span explains the alleged gain from idealism and supplies a direct causal relation between external and internal mental states.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: The sharp boundary between accessible internal states and inaccessible external mental states requires explanation rather than assumption.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan immediately isolates a premise in Bernardo's answer and asks what makes the asserted internal-external boundary.

components.text: Individual mental states are separated from the external world's mental states.
The separation permits external states to affect internal states through perception.

response.rationale: The reply squarely questions the decisive separation premise but does not independently state why failure to explain it defeats the broader causal account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It strongly contacts the decisive premise while leaving the broader consequence and causal-modulation component underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is narrowly and clearly directed at the boundary between internal and external states.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for an explanation and does not claim more than its interrogative warrant establishes.

charity.alternative: Dissociation separates personal mental states from external mental states.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply accepts that a boundary is part of the model and asks what constitutes it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory demand follows directly from the role the boundary plays in the pro causal model.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The objection is conceptually well grounded, though it supplies no competing account of individuation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the adopted subsidiary dissociation bridge rather than the complete motion-level conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately identifies the boundary premise and does not exaggerate Bernardo's claim about personal creation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span identifies the internal-external separation as an indispensable premise and asks what makes that boundary.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Bodily surfaces represent dissociative boundaries, while external mentality's intrinsic dispositions yield repeatable causal effects and preserve physical and chemical regularities.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo directly answers the boundary question and continues through a unified account of dissociation, natural selection, and predictable external states.

components.text: The account must identify what constitutes the internal-external boundary.
The boundary must connect intelligibly with bodies and their observable properties.

response.rationale: The response identifies bodily interfaces as appearances of the boundary and expands the answer into an account of selection, dispositions, and lawful predictability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly answers the boundary demand, though why dissociation initially occurs is treated as brute possibility rather than deeply explained.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-dispositional account is recoverable, but dissociation alternates between process, boundary, life, and represented biological organization.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges a brute origin, but possibility plus time does not warrant that every possible natural event is bound to occur.

charity.alternative: A bodily boundary and physical structure may require a nonidealist explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The answer preserves the importance of bodies and physical laws by treating them as representations rather than denying them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The model links boundary, selection, and dispositions coherently, but the move from possibility to inevitable dissociation is materially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Biological interfaces and regular laws are relevant examples, while the universal mental dispositions and origin story remain asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central pro bridge explaining causation and physical regularity under idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: It directly answers the embodied-boundary concern and retains the empirical validity of physics and chemistry.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span connects bodily interfaces to dissociative boundaries and intrinsic mental dispositions to predictable physical and chemical laws.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: A neutral-monist representational account avoids the hard problem by locating experience in a bat's models rather than in a separately assumed physical bat.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan explicitly identifies herself as a neutral monist and develops her alternative through the Nagel bat example.

components.text: A monist ontology can preserve causal and physical regularity without nonmental substance.
External mentality has intrinsic dispositions that explain predictable physical behavior.

response.rationale: The move supplies a relevant neutral-monist representational alternative but does not contact the selected target's specific disposition and regularity claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The contrary model is developed clearly and bears on ontology, while the immediate causal-regularity argument goes unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bat-representation proposal is recoverable, but the ontological status of representations and the neutral substrate stays partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposal is explicitly exploratory and described as avoiding rather than solving the hard problem.

charity.alternative: Idealism offers a developed monist account intended to escape the hard problem.
charity.decisiveQualification: Susan recognizes it as a strong monist attempt and does not equate it with ordinary materialism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Restricting the target of what-it-is-like claims to representations is coherent, though the bearer and substrate of representation remain implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Nagel analysis motivates the reframe, but no independent evidence establishes experience at the representational level.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially develops the con route's central representational alternative to foundational consciousness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opposing monism is acknowledged as serious and powerful before the speaker advances a distinct representational route.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span states neutral monism and develops the bat-representation reframe as a way to avoid importing a physical-object hard problem.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Representational self-models can be delusions, but their experienced existence still requires mentality and therefore does not rescue materialist illusionism.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo directly responds to Susan's representational proposal, grants its neutral-monist form, and distinguishes it from materialist illusionism.

components.text: There is something it is like to be a representation or model rather than a persisting physical self.
The representational reframe avoids the hard problem without committing to idealism.
The neutral-monist version need not claim that only neuroactivity exists.

response.rationale: The reply grants Susan's nonmaterialist model account, then argues that experienced delusions require consciousness and that neuroactivity-only versions regress to further models.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts all decisive components, preserves Susan's neutral qualification, and isolates the regress problem specifically for materialist illusionism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The span consistently distinguishes personal agents, conscious models, idealism, neutral monism, and materialist illusionism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Experienced illusion plausibly presupposes experience, but the move treats this as establishing that only consciousness exists.

charity.alternative: Susan's representational account is nonmaterialist and treats the enduring personal self as a delusive model.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bernardo expressly agrees that Susan's version avoids the hard problem because she is not a materialist or eliminativist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress objection against neuroactivity-only models is clear, though the final step from experienced delusion to idealism remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The self-model analysis and regress supply appropriate conceptual support, but they do not exclude every neutral ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the complete pro conclusion by arguing that experienced representation ultimately preserves consciousness as fundamental.

representationalCharity.rationale: It carefully distinguishes Susan's neutral-monist proposal from the materialist illusionism being criticized and grants her central point.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span grants the delusive-self model, develops the meta-model regress for materialism, and argues that experienced illusions preserve mentality.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: If experience attaches to models, consistency suggests that fleeting models throughout predictive hierarchies have something it is like to be them, not only the self-model.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan immediately responds after expressing doubt about Bernardo's final inference and develops her own distributed-model implication.

components.text: The persisting personal self is a delusive conscious model rather than a stable agent.
The experienced existence of models supports the conclusion that consciousness is ontologically fundamental.
Materialist model accounts face a regress because each explanatory model would itself be neuroactivity.

response.rationale: The reply develops issue-bearing implications of conscious modeling and self dissolution but does not answer the decisive ontological inference or regress objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers substantial contrary development and contacts the self-model premise, while leaving both decisive pro inferences unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal clearly ranges over models at multiple levels and explicitly disclaims traditional atom-level panpsychism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Consistency motivates extending experience across models, but the warrant does not establish that every low-level model has experience.

charity.alternative: Idealism treats the self as a conscious delusive model while retaining consciousness as the underlying category.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply accepts the ephemeral self-model premise but does not engage the separate argument for foundational consciousness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency argument is intelligible, but it assumes without sufficient bridge that representational status at every level entails experience.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Predictive hierarchy examples illustrate the scope, while the crucial attribution of experience to each model remains asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move advances the central con representational route, though it does not directly defeat the motion-level idealist inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly adopts the delusive-self premise but omits the decisive idealist regress and ontological qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span extends the something-it-is-like claim across fleeting predictive models and connects this view to dissolution of the self-model.
